focus: OpenCode plugin, per-runtime commands and prompts, hook registries and generated mirrors under .claude/.codex/.cursor/.devin/.pi
sourcesRead: opencode-goal.js (dispatch, normalizeOptions, state dir, status lines, kill switch, packet/log branches)
novelty: Ring 2 keeps ring 1 and adds the native plugin, the registry generator, three command surfaces, and the symlink topology. It corrects one ring-1 verdict and falsifies one of its own hypotheses.

label: resolveWorkspaceRoot is NOT dead code — the OpenCode plugin calls it
detail: Both twins are live in different implementations: the plugin uses goalSlice.resolveWorkspaceRoot, the core and Pi use resolveRepoRoot. Ring 1 could not see the plugin and read its own test-only reference as proof of death. The corrected finding is R2-F1: two live implementations of one walk, with the slice module claiming to be the single place the boundary is drawn.
novelty: a ring-1 verdict reversed by ring 2

label: Two live implementations of the workspace-root walk, in the two implementations that claim to share one boundary
detail: goal-slice.cjs states it exists so the CommonJS core and the ESM plugin cannot drift apart on the boundary. That holds for the frontmatter boundary it introduces. The workspace root, which decides which .opencode/skills tree the state dir lives under, is a second boundary drawn twice, and the two implementations take different sides.

label: OPENCODE_GOAL_STATE_DIR isolates state on four runtimes and is ignored by OpenCode, which writes to the real state root
detail: The core reads the env override between an explicit option and the repo-root default. The plugin reads an explicit option then a constant derived from its own file location, and the literal appears nowhere in it. README:180 tells operators to use temporary state-dir paths for manual probes precisely so they never touch the live tree; on OpenCode that instruction is wrong.
novelty: unreported; the plugin contract is silent about it, which is correct but does not warn the reader of the engine README

label: The plugin repeats the wrong-variable disable message
detail: Same shape as R1-F2 in the second implementation: DISABLED_ENV names the alias, the gate reads the canonical flag first.
novelty: confirms R1-F2 is systematic across both front ends

label: Disabling the goal hook disables the goal diagnostics on both front ends
detail: Ring 1 found this in the CLI and suspected a quirk. The plugin does the same: the disable check precedes history, doctor, health and packet. Two independent front ends make it a contract: the switch that stops goal behaviour also stops the reporting that would explain what it stopped.
novelty: upgrades R1-F3 from a CLI quirk to a two-front-end contract

label: The injection contract's verbatim Role line enumerates Cursor and Pi but not Devin
detail: The same section names Devin as an owner and documents its channel, and the adapter renders RuntimeLabel Devin. A reader copying the published block shape gets the wrong one for the adapter whose payload envelope differs most.

label: The Cursor hook README calls the goal hook Cursor-only while a Devin twin is registry-bound twice
detail: True of the file in the directory it describes, false as a fleet statement, and contradicted one directory over.

label: Three of the four runtime symlinks are decoration; only Pi's is a discovery path
detail: The generated registries invoke .opencode/hooks/goal/{cursor,devin}/goal-inject.mjs directly. .cursor/hooks/goal-inject.mjs and .devin/hooks/goal-inject.mjs resolve and are never executed; .opencode/hooks/goal/opencode/opencode-goal.js is documented as browsability-only. Pi is the exception: .pi/extensions/goal-context.ts is what Pi's loader discovers.

label: Claude and Codex goal support is asserted in two documents and carried by nothing in this repository
detail: No Claude goal command, no Codex goal prompt, no goal binding for either runtime in the hook registry, and no test that would fail if the host command changed. The claim is about software outside this tree. UNKNOWN whether those products currently ship the assumed surface; their own documentation would settle it.
novelty: unreported as an unverifiable claim rather than a wrong one

label: The plugin command surface is the third place to present the disable alias as the primary name
detail: The alias does work, so the instruction is not wrong; but nothing on any of the three surfaces says which name the resolver reads first.
novelty: confirms the R1-F1 class across surfaces
